CHAPTER I
SUMMARY OF SCIENCE
There ere a n~mber of forces that are independent of
acceleration fields that can generate fluid flows or affect
existing ones in the reduced gravity environment of space. For
example, surface- or interracial-tension g~adients, thermal­
volume expansions, phase change~, ~nd electri~ end magnetic
fields can induce such flows. The nature and extent of many
fluid flows in a reduced-gravity environment cannot, et present,
be predicted either because of their innate complexity or they
have not received sufficient attention.
Considering the various types of flows that can occur in
micro-gravity, it becomes readily apparent that flows induced by
surface-tension gradients are perhaps the most interesting, not
only for their inherent scientific interest, but also for their
technological applications, such as the containerless processin6
of materials in space. Furthermore, as will be indicated later,
such flows will be significantly different in apace than on earth
so that the experimentation in a spacecraft environment is
,

2
essential to identify and quantify the phenomena associated with
surface-tension gradients.
The presence of an interface bet ween t wo fluid phases can
influence the motion of fluids when either the interface has a
finite curvature which is different from tbat at equilibrium or
when the interfacial or surface tension varies spatially. Since
the surface tension is a function of temperature, composition,
and electrical potential, gradienls of any 6ne of these or
combinations of them lead to surface-tension gradients. It has
been pointed out by Ostrach (1977) that there are essentially two
basic modes of flow generated by surface-tension gradients that
are analogous to those induced by buoyancy. If the gradients are
along the interface, the surface-tension gradients act like shear
stresses applied by the interface to the adjoining fluid, and
thereby, generate flows or affect existing ones. The flows,
under certain conditions, can affect transport phenomenon. Of
the relatively little early work on problems of this type the
emphasis has been on diffusocapillary flows, caused by
concentration gradients.
If one of the above-mentioned gradients is perpendicular to

3
the interface, a Marangoni instability can occur under proper
conditions that can lead to flows analogous to the thermally
unstable buoyancy flows. Problems of this type have received
more attention than those with gradients along the interface.
The distinction between the two types or flows had not previously
been clear.
The ground-based work that has been don~ will be described
herein to indicate the basic scientific information required to
gain an understanding of surface-tension gradient induced flows
and to define a spaceflight experimental program that will yield
those results.

An extensive review made of existing work showed that the

Furthermore, the relevant parameters that characterize the

Since under reduced-gravity conditions surface-tension
gradients are a dominant force for the flow of fluids with free

1.2 Objectives
Because thermocapil lary flows represent a relatively new
subject and the spacecraft environment is al s o new, a two-step
experimental program is proposed to st udy the bas i c fluid
mechanics and heat transfer phenomena of surface-tension driven
convection at reduced gravity. The basic configurations for the
proposed experiments are shown schematically· in Fig. 1. Liquid
is placed in an open circular container and its· free surface is
subjected to a temperature gradient to induce thermocapillary
convection in the container.
The main objectives of the experiments are to investigate:
1. the extent and nature of thermocapillary
flows in transient periods as well as
under steady conditions
ii. temperature distributions along the free
surface and in the bulk fluid
111. the effect of the heating mode and the
heating level on the flows

the flows
v. the onset conditions and nature of
oscillatory flows
Two experimental series are proposed to accomplish the
above objectives. They are explained in detail in Chapter Ill.
In the first experiments the above objectives (1) to (iv) will be
accomplished and attempts will be made to obtain oscillatory
flow. The oscillation phenomenon, which is a very important
subject in the present study, is not yet fully understood.
Therefore a detailed study of the phenomenon will be done in the
second series of experiments.
